content:
In modern organizations, surveys are often viewed as a straightforward way to gather feedback and improve services. Educational institutions and corporate training departments regularly collect participant opinions to evaluate course quality, instructor effectiveness, and future training needs. However, what appears to be a simple survey can raise significant ethical concerns when examined through the lens of data science ethics.

Drawing on concepts from Martens (2022), Data Science Ethics: Concepts, Techniques, and Cautionary Tales, this blog post analyzes a course evaluation survey scenario in which participants complete an online survey after finishing a course. Although respondents are told that the survey is anonymous, they must access the survey through a web link and log in using organizational credentials. Executive management plans to use the results to determine which courses should be redesigned or updated. As the designated data analyst, it is important to recognize not only the value of the collected data but also the ethical implications surrounding its collection, storage, analysis, and use.

Participants complete a ten-question survey at the end of a course. To access the survey, they must:

• Visit a web-based survey link.

• Log in using their organizational username and password.

• Select the course being evaluated.

• Complete the survey.

The survey introduction states that responses will remain anonymous. However, because participants authenticate before responding, an immediate ethical question emerges: Can a survey truly be anonymous if users must identify themselves to gain access? Additionally, one of the survey questions asks respondents to rate a statement using a scale from “Strongly Agree” to “Strongly Disagree.” While seemingly harmless, the survey design reveals numerous ethical concerns when evaluated using data science ethics principles.

1. Ethical Issues Present in the Survey Design and Sample Question

A. Misleading Claims of Anonymity

The most obvious ethical concern is the survey’s claim that responses are anonymous while requiring authentication through organizational credentials. Even if the survey system is configured not to store usernames alongside responses, respondents may reasonably believe that their identity can still be linked to their answers. From an ethical standpoint, this creates a problem of transparency. According to ethical data practices, individuals must be informed accurately about how their data are collected and used. If respondents are led to believe that their identities cannot be connected to their responses when the system technically could allow such linkage, the survey may be considered misleading. This issue relates directly to:

• Informed consent

• Transparency

• Trustworthiness

• Data governance

When participants do not fully understand how their information is handled, their consent cannot be considered truly informed.

B. Potential Privacy Violations

Logging into the survey creates the possibility that technical data could identify respondents, including:

• Usernames

• Session identifiers

• Login logs

• IP addresses

• Device information

• Timestamp records

Even if these identifiers are not intentionally analyzed, their existence creates privacy risks.

In Martens’ framework, responsible data science requires minimizing unnecessary data collection. If organizational credentials are only needed to prevent duplicate submissions, alternative approaches may exist that collect less personally identifiable information.

This raises concerns regarding the ethical principle of privacy preservation.

C. Power Imbalance and Response Bias

Another ethical issue is the organizational relationship between respondents and management.

Employees or students may fear that negative responses could somehow be traced back to them. As a result, they may provide more favorable ratings than they actually believe.

This fear can undermine data quality by producing: • Inflated ratings

• Reduced criticism

• Lower survey honesty

• Distorted conclusions

An ethical survey should promote genuine participation without creating perceived risks for respondents.

D. Ambiguity in the Survey Question

Although the sample question uses a standard agreement scale, ethical concerns can arise if:

• The statement is vague.

• Key terms are not defined.

• Respondents interpret wording differently.

Data scientists have a responsibility to ensure that survey questions measure what they intend to measure. Poorly designed questions threaten the ethical principle of data quality because management may make important decisions based on unreliable or misunderstood responses.

E. Risk of Function Creep

Function creep occurs when data collected for one purpose are later used for another purpose without the participant’s original agreement.

Respondents are told that survey results will evaluate courses. However, if management later uses responses to evaluate instructors, departments, or specific participants, the original purpose changes.

This violates ethical expectations regarding:

• Purpose limitation

• Consent

• Fair use of data

2. Other Ethical Issues That Could Be Present

Beyond the issues explicitly described, several additional ethical risks may exist.

A. Data Security Risks

Survey data may contain sensitive comments or criticisms. If stored improperly, unauthorized individuals could gain access to identifiable information.

Questions include:

• Who can access survey data?

• How long is data retained?

• Is the information encrypted?

• Are there audit controls?

Ethical data stewardship requires strong safeguards to protect respondents.

B. Lack of Data Minimization

The survey may collect more information than necessary. Examples:

• Authentication logs

• Location data

• Browser information

• Demographic information

The principle of data minimization suggests collecting only what is necessary to achieve the stated objective.

C. Selection Bias

Only participants who complete the survey during the available time window can contribute responses. Potential consequences include:

• Underrepresentation of certain groups

• Overrepresentation of highly satisfied or dissatisfied individuals

• Distorted survey results

Biased samples lead to biased decisions, creating fairness concerns.

D. Nonresponse Bias

People with strong positive or negative opinions often participate at higher rates than individuals with neutral opinions.

If participation rates are low, executive management may receive an inaccurate picture of course quality.

Ethically, data analysts should disclose such limitations rather than present survey results as perfectly representative.

E. Re-identification Risk

Even if names are removed from survey responses, participants can sometimes be identified through combinations of information such as:

• Course attended

• Completion date

• Department

• Unique comments

This is known as re-identification risk, one of the most discussed issues in modern data ethics.

True anonymity is difficult to guarantee when datasets can be linked with other organizational records.

F. Lack of Accountability

An additional concern is whether the organization has established accountability mechanisms. Questions include:

• Who oversees survey ethics?

• Who validates anonymity claims?

• Who approves secondary data uses?

Without accountability structures, ethical promises may not be enforceable.

3. Recommendations to Executive Management

To address these ethical concerns, several improvements should be implemented.

Recommendation 1: Be Honest About Anonymity

If authentication occurs, the survey should not automatically be described as anonymous.

Instead, the organization should clearly explain:

• Why login is required

• What data are collected

• Whether usernames are stored

• How responses are separated from identities

Transparency builds trust and supports informed consent.

Recommendation 2: Adopt Privacy-by-Design Principles

Privacy should be built into the survey process from the beginning.

Possible measures include:

• Separating login records from survey responses

• Removing identifiers before analysis

• Encrypting stored data

• Restricting administrative access

These approaches reduce privacy risks while maintaining analytical usefulness.

Recommendation 3: Improve Consent Language

The survey introduction should clearly disclose:

• Survey objectives

• Data retention periods

• Access permissions

• Potential reporting uses

Participants should understand exactly how their information will be used.

Recommendation 4: Conduct an Ethical Risk Assessment

Before launching the survey, management should evaluate:

• Privacy risks

• Security vulnerabilities

• Re-identification risks

• Potential biases

This aligns with responsible data governance practices.

Recommendation 5: Improve Survey Design

Questions should be reviewed to ensure:

• Neutral wording

• Clear terminology

• Accessibility

• Lack of leading language

Higher-quality questions improve both ethics and decision-making.

Recommendation 6: Publish Aggregate Results Only

Reports should focus on aggregated outcomes rather than individual responses.

Examples include:

• Course-level averages

• Trend analysis

• Department-wide findings

Aggregation helps preserve anonymity while still providing valuable business insights.

Recommendation 7: Establish Governance and Accountability

Management should create formal policies governing:

• Data access

• Data retention

• Secondary use restrictions

• Compliance monitoring

Strong governance supports ethical data science throughout the survey lifecycle.

4. How Could a Data Analyst Proceed Ethically if Management Rejects These Recommendations?

Unfortunately, ethical conflicts sometimes arise when organizational leaders dismiss concerns.

If executive management insists that the survey is acceptable despite identified issues, several ethical options remain available.

A. Document Concerns Professionally

The analyst should create written documentation describing:

• Identified risks

• Ethical implications

• Recommended mitigations

This ensures transparency and demonstrates professional diligence.

B. Continue Advocating Through Evidence

Rather than framing objections as personal opinions, the analyst can present:

• Privacy principles

• Data governance standards

• Industry best practices

• Ethical frameworks from the literature

Evidence-based discussions are more likely to influence decision-makers.

C. Limit Misleading Claims

If reporting survey results, the analyst should avoid overstating conclusions.

For example:

• Acknowledge response limitations.

• Discuss possible biases.

• Clarify anonymity uncertainties.

Professional integrity requires honest communication.

D. Seek Guidance from Ethics or Compliance Officers

If available, concerns can be elevated to:

• Ethics committees

• Privacy officers

• Legal departments

• Compliance teams

This allows broader organizational review of identified risks.

E. Follow Professional Codes of Conduct

Data professionals have ethical responsibilities that extend beyond management preferences.

Principles such as:

• Honesty

• Fairness

• Accountability

• Respect for privacy

should guide decision-making.

F. Consider Whistleblower Protections if Necessary

In extreme situations involving serious legal or ethical violations, formal reporting channels may be appropriate. Such actions should follow organizational policies and applicable laws.

Conclusion

At first glance, this course evaluation survey appears to be a routine feedback mechanism. However, a deeper ethical analysis reveals substantial concerns regarding anonymity, privacy, transparency, data quality, bias, and accountability. The requirement that participants log in while simultaneously being told that responses are anonymous creates an especially important tension that may undermine both trust and data integrity.

Using concepts from Martens’ Data Science Ethics, we can identify several relevant ethical principles, including informed consent, transparency, privacy preservation, data minimization, accountability, fairness, data quality, governance, re-identification risk, and purpose limitation. These concepts demonstrate that ethical data science is not merely about collecting information but about ensuring that collection, analysis, and use of data respect the rights and expectations of the individuals providing it.

Ultimately, organizations obtain better insights when participants trust the process. Ethical survey design is therefore not only the right thing to do, but also a practical strategy for generating more reliable data, better decisions, and stronger organizational credibility.
title: Anonymous… or Not? The Ethics of Course Surveys in a Data-Driven Organization

content:
Can artificial intelligence make medicines safer? Increasingly, the answer appears to be yes. Yet as machine learning transforms pharmacovigilance and drug safety, an important ethical question emerges: who governs the algorithms that help protect patients? While laws and regulations provide an essential foundation, they often struggle to keep pace with rapidly evolving AI technologies. This gap highlights the growing importance of soft ethics, a complementary approach that promotes responsible innovation beyond legal compliance.

Introduction: AI’s Expanding Role in Drug Safety

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are revolutionizing pharmacovigilance, the science of detecting, assessing, understanding, and preventing adverse effects of medicines. Pharmaceutical companies, regulatory agencies, and healthcare organizations increasingly use ML algorithms to process large volumes of adverse event reports, identify safety signals, predict drug-related risks, and improve decision-making.

Organizations such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the European Medicines Agency (EMA), and major pharmaceutical companies are exploring AI-powered systems to enhance patient safety. Machine learning can analyze millions of records far faster than human reviewers, enabling earlier detection of potential safety concerns.

However, the deployment of AI in drug safety introduces significant ethical challenges. Regulatory frameworks often lag behind technological advancements, making it difficult to ensure that AI systems remain transparent, fair, accountable, and trustworthy. Data-driven technologies can create ethical risks that extend beyond legal requirements. This is where soft ethics becomes particularly valuable.

This blog explores the ethical challenges of machine learning in pharmacovigilance, examines the limitations of current AI regulation, and discusses how soft ethics can help address governance gaps.

Machine Learning Applications in Pharmacovigilance

Pharmacovigilance traditionally relies on human experts reviewing Individual Case Safety Reports (ICSRs), scientific literature, electronic health records, and post-marketing surveillance data. Machine learning expands these capabilities by automating many labor-intensive processes.

Common applications include:

1. Adverse Event Detection

Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithms can extract adverse event information from physician notes, patient reports, social media posts, and medical literature.

2. Signal Detection

Machine learning models can identify unusual reporting patterns that may indicate previously unknown drug safety risks.

3. Case Prioritization

AI systems can classify and prioritize safety reports for human review, reducing workload and improving efficiency.

4. Predictive Risk Assessment

Algorithms can estimate which patient populations may be more vulnerable to adverse drug reactions based on demographic, clinical, and genetic factors.

These applications have tremendous potential to improve public health. However, greater capability also creates greater ethical responsibility.

The Limits of Regulation

Regulation remains a cornerstone of responsible AI deployment. Governments worldwide are developing AI governance frameworks to address risks associated with automated decision-making.

Despite these efforts, regulation faces several limitations.

Regulation Is Reactive Rather Than Proactive

Technology evolves much faster than legislation.

Machine learning models can be developed, deployed, and updated within months, whereas regulatory changes often take years. By the time lawmakers address one issue, new technologies may have introduced entirely different ethical concerns.

In pharmacovigilance, AI systems may continuously learn from incoming data. Regulators often struggle to evaluate dynamic systems that change over time.

Global Inconsistency

AI governance varies significantly across jurisdictions.

For example:

• The European Union has adopted comprehensive AI regulations emphasizing risk-based oversight.

• The United States generally relies on sector-specific regulations.

• Other countries remain in earlier stages of AI governance development.

Pharmaceutical companies operating globally may face inconsistent expectations regarding transparency, accountability, and privacy.

Difficulty Assessing Algorithmic Complexity

Many machine learning systems function as “black boxes.”

Deep learning models can generate predictions without providing easily understandable explanations. Regulators may find it difficult to determine:

• Why a particular safety signal was identified.

• Whether bias influenced outcomes.

• How errors might affect patient safety.

Traditional regulatory methods were not designed for highly complex, adaptive algorithms.

Compliance Does Not Guarantee Ethical Behavior

Perhaps the most important limitation is that legal compliance and ethical responsibility are not the same thing.

An AI system may fully comply with applicable regulations while still producing harmful outcomes due to bias, poor design decisions, or inadequate oversight.

This distinction reflects a major theme throughout Data Science Ethics: ethical responsibility must extend beyond simply following the law.

Key Ethical Risks in AI-Driven Pharmacovigilance

Several ethical concepts studied throughout the course are particularly relevant to AI applications in drug safety.

1. Bias and Fairness

Bias occurs when algorithms systematically disadvantage certain groups.

A machine learning model trained primarily on data from specific populations may perform poorly for underrepresented groups.

For example:

• Rare disease patients may be overlooked.

• Minority populations may be underrepresented in safety datasets.

• Algorithmic predictions may not reflect diverse patient experiences.

Fairness requires ensuring that AI systems produce equitable outcomes across populations.

2. Transparency

Transparency refers to the ability to understand how a system functions and reaches decisions.

In pharmacovigilance, regulators, healthcare providers, and pharmaceutical companies need confidence that AI-generated safety findings are reliable.

Without transparency, stakeholders may struggle to trust AI recommendations.

3. Accountability

When an AI system misses a serious adverse safety signal, who is responsible? Potentially:

• Software developers

• Pharmaceutical companies

• Regulatory agencies

• Safety reviewers

Accountability mechanisms become blurred when decision-making is partially automated.

Establishing clear responsibility remains a critical ethical requirement.

4. Privacy

Machine learning often relies on large datasets containing sensitive health information.

Ethical data science requires:

• Data minimization

• Secure storage

• Appropriate consent practices

• Protection against re-identification risks

Patient privacy remains fundamental to maintaining public trust.

5. Explainability

Explainability differs from transparency by focusing on the ability to communicate specific AI decisions in understandable terms.

Healthcare professionals are unlikely to trust recommendations they cannot interpret.

Explainable AI helps bridge the gap between algorithmic outputs and human judgment.

A Real-World Example: IBM Watson for Oncology

One widely discussed example illustrating the challenges of AI governance in healthcare is IBM Watson for Oncology.

Watson was developed to assist clinicians by recommending cancer treatment options using machine learning and medical knowledge databases.

Although the system generated significant excitement, reports later revealed concerns regarding reliability, transparency, and real-world performance. Critics argued that some recommendations were not sufficiently supported by clinical evidence and that decision-making processes were difficult to understand.

Importantly, many of these concerns were not necessarily violations of regulations. Rather, they highlighted broader ethical issues related to:

• Transparency

• Explainability

• Accountability

• Human oversight

The Watson experience demonstrates that regulatory compliance alone does not guarantee trustworthy AI.

It also illustrates why healthcare organizations must consider ethical principles throughout the AI lifecycle, from design and development to deployment and monitoring.

The Role of Soft Ethics

Soft ethics refers to ethical principles, professional standards, best practices, and voluntary governance mechanisms that operate beyond minimum legal requirements.

Rather than asking, “What are we legally allowed to do?” soft ethics asks, “What is the responsible thing to do?”

This approach aligns closely with the principles discussed throughout Data Science Ethics.

Soft Ethics as a Complement to Regulation

Soft ethics does not replace regulation.

Instead, it helps address areas where laws are incomplete, outdated, or insufficiently detailed.

Examples include:

• Professional codes of conduct

• Ethical review boards

• Responsible AI frameworks

• Industry best practices

• Organizational ethics committees

These mechanisms can evolve more quickly than legislation.

Encouraging Ethical-by-Design Development

Soft ethics promotes integrating ethical considerations during system design rather than after deployment.

For pharmacovigilance AI systems, organizations can:

• Conduct bias assessments

• Evaluate societal impacts

• Perform algorithmic audits

• Include multidisciplinary review teams

• Document ethical decision-making processes

This proactive approach reduces the likelihood of future harm.

Strengthening Trust

Trust is essential in healthcare and drug safety.

Patients must trust that their data are handled responsibly.

Healthcare professionals must trust AI recommendations.

Regulators must trust safety evaluations.

Soft ethics contributes to trustworthiness by emphasizing:

• Integrity

• Transparency

• Responsibility

• Respect for persons

These values support long-term acceptance of AI technologies.

Applying Data Science Ethics Principles to AI Systems

The ethical principles provide a practical framework for AI governance in pharmacovigilance.

Beneficence

AI systems should promote patient well-being and improve public health outcomes.

Non-Maleficence

Organizations should actively identify and minimize risks of harm caused by algorithmic errors or biased predictions.

Justice and Fairness

Models should be evaluated across diverse populations to prevent inequitable outcomes.

Respect for Autonomy

Patients should understand how their data are used and retain appropriate control over personal information.

Accountability

Clear governance structures must define responsibility for AI-enabled decisions.

Transparency and Explainability

Stakeholders should be able to understand how AI systems operate and how conclusions are reached.

Collectively, these principles create a foundation for ethical AI that extends beyond technical performance measures.

The global landscape of AI ethics guidelines. Nature Machine Intelligence, 1(9), 389-399. https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-019-0088-2 Kelleher, J. D., & Tierney, B. (2018). Data science. MIT Press.

Mittelstadt, B. D. (2019). Principles alone cannot guarantee ethical AI. Nature Machine Intelligence, 1(11), 501-507. https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-019-0114-4

title: Beyond Compliance: Machine Learning in Pharmacovigilance and Drug Safety and the Limits of AI Regulation

Opcionalmente, habilita esto por página agregando mathjax: true a tu frontmatter.

Soporte de Emoji

La función emojify se puede llamar directamente en las plantillas o Shortcodes en línea.

Para habilitar emoji globalmente, establece enableEmoji en true en la configuración de tu sitio y luego puedes escribir códigos abreviados de emoji directamente en los archivos de contenido; por ejemplo:

La Hoja de trucos de Emoji es una referencia útil para los códigos abreviados de emoji.

N.B. Los pasos anteriores habilitan los caracteres y secuencias de emoji del Estándar Unicode en Hugo, sin embargo, la representación de estos glifos depende del navegador y la plataforma. Para estilizar los emoji, puedes usar una fuente de emoji de terceros o una pila de fuentes; por ejemplo:

.emoji {
  font-family: Apple Color Emoji, Segoe UI Emoji, NotoColorEmoji, Segoe UI Symbol, Android Emoji, EmojiSymbols;
}

Le Canon de Van de Graaf

Mane refeci capiebant unda mulcebat

Victa caducifer, malo vulnere contra dicere aurato, ludit regale, voca! Retorsit colit est profanae esse virescere furit nec; iaculi matertera et visa est, viribus. Mentefque cum suae pelle

Viscera tot vagina, mihi est Theseus! Obstruat pede! Concita tamen, cum et vulnera croceo aegide tetigere deducit. Est quis vultus fata, scelus paratae inter agmen spectat fuit, Thisbe vulnera vellet laniarat, arva paludibus!

Dixit exarsit nocens, dextra secum ira columbae: Proponas, in pinus et alis dea atque. Aeneas, certum possent, temeraria, umeris colla in quoque. Interea fugit inpediunt nocet.

Praecipites nescio Titania tetigit, nunc volentem sua pectora nec, exstinctum Pylius undas. Agro. Dumque in est moenia vidi, vinci dat acervos precatur bracchia et modo et quos cum illas solvet, dum fecit.
